title: Earthquakes, Volcanoes and Tsunamis

cards.h: The Earth moves, and people die
cards.b: Quakes, volcanoes and tsunamis appear both in Physical Geography and in disaster management. India has had Latur (1993), Bhuj (2001), the 2004 tsunami and Nepal (2015). UPSC asks about causes, distribution and India's exposure.

Stress builds on a fault. Rock slips, and energy spreads as waves. Magnitude (Richter, now usually the moment scale) is logarithmic: each step is about 10 times the wave amplitude and about 32 times the energy. Intensity (Mercalli, I to XII) measures effects felt.
Quakes mostly follow plate boundaries. Shallow quakes happen at all boundaries. Deep ones only occur in subduction zones. Intraplate quakes (Latur, Bhuj) are rarer, along old buried faults.

Volcanic quakes, collapse quakes (mines, caves) and reservoir-induced quakes also occur. The Koyna quake of 1967 (about M6.3) is the classic Indian case of reservoir-induced seismicity.

Effects: ground shaking, liquefaction, landslides, fires, tsunamis. The shaking and poor building, not the quake itself, kills most people.

A volcano is a vent where magma reaches the surface. Shield volcanoes (Mauna Loa) are broad with runny basalt. Composite cones (Fuji, Vesuvius) alternate lava and ash and are explosive. Caldera (Krakatoa, Toba) forms when a cone collapses. Flood basalts built the Deccan Traps.

Magma cooling underground makes batholiths (big domes), laccoliths (lens with a flat base), sills (horizontal sheets) and dykes (vertical walls). Dykes are common in the Deccan. Surface forms include cones, lava plateaus and geysers and hot springs from heated ground water.

Volcano status: active, dormant or extinct.

A tsunami (Japanese for harbour wave) is a series of waves from a sudden seabed shift, usually from a subduction quake, landslide or eruption. It is hardly seen in deep water. On reaching shallows it slows and rises.

Hunga Tonga (2022) showed that eruptions can cause them too.

cards.h: India's seismic map and the 2004 tsunami
cards.b:
The long-used BIS map (IS 1893, 2002) has four zones, II to V, with Zone V the highest. About 59% of India's land is quake-prone. A revised BIS code released in November 2025 adds a new Zone VI for the Himalayan arc, so check which map a question refers to.

On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1-9.3 quake off Sumatra sent waves to Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. India then set up the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007).

No. Science can give probabilities and hazard maps, not exact times. Early-warning systems exploit the gap between fast P waves and damaging S waves, giving seconds of notice.

Real risk reduction comes from building codes, retrofitting, land-use rules and drills. After Bhuj (26 January 2001, M7.7) and Nepal (25 April 2015, M7.8) the debate shifted from nature to unsafe construction.

Likely questions

"Describe the distribution of volcanoes and earthquakes in the world." (10 marks)

"Why is the Himalayan region prone to earthquakes? How do they differ from the Peninsular ones?" (15 marks)

Structure: define; give causes; map the Pacific and Alpine belts; add Indian zones; end with mitigation (codes, early warning, drills).

Prelims tip: Richter is logarithmic; Mercalli measures intensity; Barren Island is India's only active volcano; Koyna is the reservoir-induced example.

quiz.w: Sills are horizontal; dykes cut across layers.
Fuji alternates lava and ash. Mauna Loa is a shield.

quiz.q: On the 2002 BIS seismic map, which zone was the most severe?
quiz.w: Zone V, covering Kashmir, the northeast and Kutch. The 2025 revision adds a Zone VI for the Himalayan arc.

quiz.w: It began in 2007 after the 2004 disaster.
